﴿Woe to those who give less [than due]﴾ ﴿who, when they take a measure from people, take it in full﴾ ﴿but when they measure or weigh for them, they give less﴾. Opening the surah with the word "woe" (wayl) signals that it contains a threat expressed with the word wayl, which is an element of eloquent opening (bara'at al-istihlal). A similar example is His saying, ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ [al-Masad: 1]. Abu Bakr ibn al-Khazin took from its reverse the opening of a poem he composed congratulating someone on the birth of a child:

"Good news! Fortune has fulfilled what it promised."

Al-tatfif (giving less than due) is falling short of the rightful quantity in what is weighed or measured. It is the verbal noun of ṭaffafa, when one reaches the ṭufāfa. Al-ṭufāf, with a damma on the ṭā' and a light fā', is what falls short of filling a vessel with drink or food; it is also said al-ṭaff with a fatha on the ṭā' without the feminine ending. All three forms are applied to what exceeds the rim of the measure of what is being filled, and it is only a small surplus above what fills the vessel; hence it is called ṭufāfa, meaning a small excess.

We do not know a simple (unaugmented) verb for it, since it is only transmitted in the form of tafʿīl, its verb being ṭaffafa. It seems they took into account in the tafʿīl form the sense of effort and attempt, because the one who gives less tries to diminish the measure without the one receiving it being aware. Its opposite is wafāʾ (full measure).

Wayl (woe) is a word of supplication for a bad condition; in the Qur'an it is a threat of punishment and reproach. Wayl is a noun, not a verbal noun, because there is no verb for it. It was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79], in Surat al-Baqarah.

This is the practice of those who position themselves for trade, seizing on people's need to buy from them and to sell to them; for merchants are the owners of capital, and the measures and scales are in their hands. The people of Mecca were merchants, and in Yathrib there were also merchants, including Jews such as Abu Rafi' and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, the two merchants of the people of the Hijaz. Their trade was in dates and grains. The people of Mecca dealt by weight, because they traded in various kinds of goods and weighed gold and silver; the people of Yathrib dealt by measure.

The verse indicates that giving less was widespread in Medina at the beginning of the period of the Hijra, and the mixing of the Muslims with the hypocrites caused this.

The exegetes agreed that the people of Yathrib were among the most corrupt of people in measuring. A group of exegetes said: this verse was revealed concerning them, and afterwards they improved their measuring. Ibn Majah related it from Ibn 'Abbas.

Among those famous for giving less in Medina was a man called by the kunya Abu Juhayna, whose name was 'Amr. He had two ṣā's: he took with one and gave with the other.

The clause ﴿Those who, when they take a measure from people, take it in full﴾ is an incidental insertion (idmāj), brought to expose a blameworthy habit in them: eagerness to get the full amount of what they buy, without any right to it. The intended point is the clause coordinated with it, namely ﴿but when they measure or weigh for them, they give less﴾; thus they are blamed for the combination of both clauses.

Al-ikhtiyāl (taking a measure) is an iftiʿāl form from kayl (measuring). It is used for receiving what is measured, in the manner of the usage of the verbs ibtāʿa (bought), irtahana (took a pledge), and ishtarā (purchased), in the sense of taking the item sold, taking the pledged thing, and taking the purchased goods. It is thus the intransitive counterpart (muṭāwiʿ) of kāla, just as ibtāʿa is the counterpart of bāʿa, irtahana of rahana, and ishtarā of sharā. He said, ﴿So send with us our brother, and we will take a measure﴾ [Yusuf: 63], meaning we will take food by measure; then the sense of the intransitive counterpart was forgotten from it.

The proper usage of iktāla is to be transitive to one object, the thing measured, so one says iktāla fulān ṭaʿāman, like ibtāʿa. It is made to take an additional object by a particle such as min of origin, so one says iktāla ṭaʿāman min fulān. In the verse it is governed by ʿalā because iktālū implies the sense of imposition (taḥāmul), i.e., laying hardship on another and wronging him. That is because the merchant's nature and character is to seek to maximize profit, and it is the place of abundance and of money being in his hand; so he exploits the need of the one who comes to him with the goods. On the authority of al-Farrāʾ, ʿalā and min alternate in this context: since it is a right upon him, when one says iktaltu ʿalayka, it is as if he said: I took what is upon you; and when he says iktaltu minka, it is like his saying istawfaytu minka.

So the meaning of ﴿they take a measure from people﴾ is: they buy from people what is sold by measure, and the object is omitted because it is known from the verb iktālū, i.e., they take a measure of something measured. The meaning of kālūhum is: they sold to people something measured, and the object is omitted because it is known.

Thus the two waws in ﴿kālūhum aw wazanūhum﴾ refer to the relative pronoun (alladhīna), and the separate pronouns refer to the people.

The verbs kālū and wazanū are made to take the pronouns by omitting the preposition lām. The original is kālū lahum and wazanū lahum, just as the lām was omitted in His saying in Surat al-Baqarah, ﴿And if you wish to have your children nursed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233], meaning to have nurses for your children, and in their proverb, "The greedy one hunts you, not the generous one," meaning the greedy one hunts for you. This is a frequent deletion, as in their saying nasahtuka and shakartuka, originally nasahtu laka and shakartu laka; for the verb kāla and the verb wazana do not take an object directly except the thing measured or weighed; one says kāla lahu ṭaʿāman and wazana lahu fiḍḍatan. Because of its frequent occurrence on the tongue, they lightened it, saying kālahu and wazanahu ṭaʿāman, by deletion and direct attachment.

Al-Farrāʾ said: it is from the speech of the people of the Hijaz and those neighbouring them of Qays, who say yakīlunā, meaning they say also kāla lahu and wazana lahu. He intends that people other than the Hijaz and Qays do not say kāla lahu and wazana lahu, but only kālahu and wazanahu; so the verb kāla among them is like bāʿa.

The restriction to His saying ﴿when they take a measure﴾ rather than saying "and when they take a weight" (wa-idhā ittazanū), as He said ﴿but when they measure or weigh for them﴾, is a substitution of the mention of weighing in the second clause, avoiding the verb ittazanū because of its infrequent use in speech, so that it would have some heaviness. There is another subtle point: the defrauders are the people of trade, and they usually take goods from the importers by measure, since the importers bring dates, wheat and the like, which are measured, and they give them prices in coin by weight, of gold or silver, minted or unminted. Therefore, in their purchases from the importers, the verb is restricted to iktiyāl, in view of what usually happens; and in their selling to buyers, measure and weight are mentioned, because they sell things by measure and receive the prices by weight. In this there is an indication that giving less was the practice of their merchants.

Yastawfūna is the answer of idhā, and istīfāʾ is taking a thing in full; the sīn and tā' in it are for intensifying the action, like istajāba.

The meaning of yukhsirūna is: they cause those for whom they measured or weighed to incur loss; and khasāra is a loss of wealth in transactions.

This verse is a warning to the Muslims against being lax about giving less, since they found it widespread in Medina at the beginning of their migration, and it is a rebuke of the polytheists among the people of Medina and the people of Mecca.

It is enough that giving less combines injustice, embezzlement and baseness, and the Arabs used to be ashamed of each of these qualities when taken separately and would disown them, yet then they would commit them all together; and that is sufficient evidence of their depravity.

﴿Do they not think that they will be raised again﴾ ﴿for a tremendous day﴾ ﴿the day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾. This is a resumptive clause (*istinaf*) arising from the threat and reproach directed at them, with the words "woe" for cheating and for what they were described as: aggressing against the rights of those who buy from them.

The hamza is for interrogation expressing astonishment, such that the questioner asks about their knowledge of the Resurrection. This indicates that the address in His saying ﴿Woe to the cheaters﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 1] is directed at the Muslims. The denial and astonishment at this refers to the denial of what this passage was brought for, namely the act of cheating (*tatfif*). As for sincere Muslims, there is no doubt that they have refrained from cheating, unlike the hypocrites.

The word *zann* (thinking) is used in its literal, well-known meaning, which is the belief that something will occur with a stronger likelihood, in the manner of His saying: ﴿We only think a thought, and we are not certain﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 32].

In the shift from the pronoun to the demonstrative in His saying ﴿Do not those ones think﴾ is intended to single them out and publicize their mention in a context of blame. Also, pointing to them after describing them as *al-Mutaffifin* indicates that the description is kept in view in the pointing, and this implies the reason for the denial.

The *lam* in His saying ﴿for a tremendous day﴾ is the *lam* of time, like His saying ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [al-Isra': 78].

The benefit of the *lam* of time is the incorporation of a response to their doubt, which led them to deny the Resurrection, based on their belief that if there were a resurrection, the dead of past generations would have been raised. So His saying "for a day" hints that the Resurrection has a specified time at which it occurs, not before it.

Describing a day as *tremendous* is by reference to the greatness of the terrors that occur in it, so it is a metaphorical attribution in the rational sense (*majazi 'aqli*).

﴿The day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for "a tremendous day," a corresponding substitution (*badal mutabiq*), and its ending is a fixed vowel (*fathat bina'*), like what was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿The day when no soul will have power for another soul at all﴾ [al-Infitar: 19] in the Surah of al-Infitar, according to the reading of the majority, who read it with a *fatha*.

The meaning of ﴿mankind stands﴾ is that they will be standing, so the use of the present tense is to bring the state vividly to mind.

The *lam* in ﴿before the Lord of the worlds﴾ is for purpose, meaning: for the sake of His lordship and receiving His judgment.

﴿Kallā﴾ (Nay!)

It is a repudiation and a rebuke of what the phrase ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 4] contains by way of amazement at their act of defrauding in measure. ﴿Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin.﴾ ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ ﴿It is a written record.﴾

This is an independent resumptive sentence, occasioned by the mention of the Day of Resurrection. It is an allusive threat to those who give short measure, that their deeds make it necessary for their record to be entered into the register of the wicked.

The term "al-fujjar" (the wicked) has come to refer to the polytheists, and to whoever might be engaged in defrauding in measure after hearing the prohibition against it from the Muslims, which some of them may have practised in the Jahiliyyah.

The definite article in "al-fujjar" is generic, intended to encompass all, that is, all the polytheists, so it includes those who give short measure and those who do not. The description "the wicked" here is similar to what is in His saying: ﴿Those are the disbelievers, the wicked﴾ [Abasa: 42].

That the generality of "the wicked" includes all polytheists, both those who defraud in measure and those who do not, is intended to indicate that those who defraud among them are the primary object of this generality, because the mention of this attribute and the threat upon it directly after the word of repudiation concerning the deeds of those who defraud is an indication that the threat is directed at them.

"Al-kitab" means the written thing, that is, the scroll, and here it may refer to a thing in which deeds are recorded, or it may be a metonym for the counting of their deeds and their being held accountable for them. In the same way, both interpretations apply to His saying: ﴿It is a written record﴾, and its parallels have been mentioned more than once before.

"Sijjin": its root letters are from the letters of Arabic, and its pattern is from Arabic patterns, so it is an Arabic word. Whoever claims that it is a loanword has erred. It is reported from al-Asma'i that the Arabs used "Sijjin" in place of "Siltin," and "Siltin" is a non-Arabic word.

The nun of "Sijjin" is original and not substituted from a lam. Its meaning has been disputed in several opinions, the most famous and most preferable of which is that it is a proper name for a valley in Hell, formed on the pattern fa'il from the root of imprisonment (sajn), for emphasis, like: "al-malik al-dilli" (the utterly misguided king), "rajul sikkir" (a man who drinks heavily), and "ta'am harif" (a very pungent food), whose pungency is the burning of the tongue. That place was named Sijjin because it is the most severe confinement for those in it, so they never leave it. This name is one of the technical terms of the Qur'an, not known in the speech of the Arabs before; but its root and pattern are established in Arabic in a generic manner. The Arabs did hear this name and did not criticize its Arabicness.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, in Sijjin﴾, if the adverbial sense is taken in its apparent meaning, the meaning is that the records of the deeds of the wicked are deposited in a place named Sijjin or described as Sijjin, and this indicates its belittlement, that is, the belittling of what it contains of their recorded deeds. Many of the early scholars took it in this sense, and al-Tabari related with his chain a hadith traced to the Prophet which supports this, but it is a munkar hadith because its chain includes unknown narrators.

If the adverbial sense in His saying "in Sijjin" is taken other than in its apparent meaning, so that the record of the wicked is figuratively described as being placed within Sijjin, meaning that the deeds counted therein are placed in Sijjin, then this is a symbolic metonym for the wicked being in Sijjin.

The clause ﴿And what will make you know what Sijjin is?﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the clause ﴿Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾ and the clause ﴿It is a written record﴾. It is a magnification of the matter of Sijjin, a magnification of horror at the state of those who are in it. ﴿What will make you know﴾ has preceded in Surat al-Infitar.

His saying ﴿It is a written record﴾ is a predicate of an elided pronoun which refers back to ﴿the record of the wicked﴾. The estimated meaning: "It, that is, the record of the wicked, is a written record." This is an ellipsis of the subject, which the Arabs follow in omitting when they speak of something and then wish to give a new predicate about it.

"Al-marqum" means written in a clear writing resembling the embroidery in a woven garment.

This description serves to emphasize what the word "kitab" conveys, whether the word is used literally or figuratively.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 83, verses 10–13:**

﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers,﴾ ﴿who deny the Day of Judgment.﴾ ﴿None deny it except every transgressor, sinful.﴾ ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Fables of the ancients."﴾

The clause ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ may be explanatory of the content of the clause ﴿Do they not think that they will be resurrected for a tremendous Day?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 4]. The phrase "that Day" (*yawma'idhin*), through its tanwin (nunation, *tanwin*), implies an omitted clause for which the tanwin serves as a substitute (*'iwad*). Its estimated form is: "On the Day when mankind stands before the Lord of the worlds, woe therein to the deniers."

It may also be an independent (*ibtida'iyya*) clause. Between "the deniers of the Day of Judgment" and "the defrauders" there is a partial general and specific relationship (*'umum wa khusus wajhi*). Some deniers are defrauders, and some defrauders are Muslims and People of the Book who do not deny the Day of Judgment. Thus this clause would be a case of interweaving (*idmaj*), threatening the polytheists who deny the Day of Judgment, even if they are not among the defrauders.

The deniers were mentioned in general terms in His saying "to the deniers," and then were restated in detail by specifying the object of their denial, which is ﴿the Day of Judgment﴾, to reinforce the establishment of their denial in the minds of the listeners, both from among them and from others, namely the Muslims and the People of the Book. The description here serves as a threat and a warning to the Muslim defrauders, lest they treat defrauding lightly and thus become like those who deny the recompense for it.

The meaning of denying "the Day of Judgment" is denying its occurrence.

Denial of the Day of Recompense is thus the source of the undertaking of evil deeds and crimes. For this reason He follows it with His saying: ﴿None deny it except every transgressor, sinful.﴾ ﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Fables of the ancients."﴾

That is, their denial of it is ignorance of the wisdom of God Most High in His creation and in imposing obligations upon them, for the wisdom behind creating humankind requires that their deeds be improved and their order be preserved. Therefore the revealed laws came to them, commanding righteousness and forbidding corruption. He also arranged for them a recompense for their righteous deeds in the form of reward and honor, and for their evil deeds in the form of punishment and humiliation, each according to his deeds. Had the Creator neglected to set right His creatures and neglected the recompense of the righteous and the corrupt, that would not be in keeping with the wisdom of creation. God Most High said: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115] ﴿Exalted is Allah, the True King.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 116].

Three attributes are mentioned for the deniers of the Day of Judgment: "transgressor" (*mu'tadin*), "sinful" (*athim*), and one who says that the verses are "fables of the ancients."

Transgression (*i'tida'*) is injustice, and the transgressor (*al-mu'tadi*) is the polytheist and the disbeliever with regard to what the revealed laws brought, because they transgressed against God by associating partners with Him, and against His messengers by denying them, and they transgressed against the evidences of the truth by not reflecting upon them or not acting upon them.

The sinful (*athim*) is an intensive form of the one who sins, that is, one who commits much sin.

The restrictive form (*qasr*) produced by negation and exception ("none... except") restricts the attribute of denying the Day of Judgment to the transgressing sinners who claim that the Qur'an is "fables of the ancients."

This is the restriction of an attribute to a qualified subject, and it is a real restriction (*qasr haqiqi*), because none deny the Day of Judgment except those who are not religious, namely the polytheists, idolaters, and their like who combine the three attributes, the greatest of which is denying the Qur'an. For the People of the Book and the Sabians do not deny the Day of Judgment, and many of the polytheists do not deny the Day of Judgment either, such as the adherents of the Coptic religion.

Those who deny the Day of Judgment are therefore the polytheists of the Arabs and those who resemble them, such as the materialists (*al-dahriyyun*, those who deny a Creator and attribute events to time). The first and second attributes, namely transgression and sin, are fully realized in them, and this is evident. As for their claim that the Qur'an is "fables of the ancients," this is the saying of the polytheists among the Arabs, and they are the primary intended target. ﴿Kalla, bal ran 'ala qulubihim ma kanu yaksibun.﴾ ﴿Kalla.﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 15].

This is an interjected statement (i'tiraD) of rebuke (radc), and it explains that rebuke. Kalla is a rebuke of their saying, "Fables of the ancients" (asatir al-awwalin), meaning: their saying is false.

The particle bal serves to negate, emphasizing the content of kalla, and to explain and reveal what led them to say what they said about the Qur'an, and that their deeds had blinded their insight with ran.

Al-Rayn is the rust that covers the blade of a sword and a mirror. The verbal noun of ran is said to be al-ran, like al-'ayb and al-'ab, and al-dhaym and al-dhamm.

The original usage of the verb is to attach it to the thing that has been struck by rayn, so one says: "ran al-sayf" and "ran al-thawb," when it has been struck by rayn, meaning it has become possessed of rayn. Because of the sense of covering that it contains, it was applied to covering in general, and from this came the verb "ran" with the meaning of "overcame," so they say: "ran al-nu'as 'ala fulan" (sleep overcame so-and-so) and "raynat al-khamr" (the wine overcame [the mind]). Likewise His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ran 'ala qulubihim﴾ is from the same usage as "ran al-rayn 'ala al-sayf." From the Qur'an's usage of this verb, people came to say: "ruyina 'ala qalb fulan" and "fulan marin 'ala qalbihi."

The meaning is: their deeds covered their hearts so that the understanding of the Qur'an could not enter them, and the vast gap between it and the fables of the ancients.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read with the assimilation (idgham) of the lam into the ra' after the lam was changed into a ra', because their points of articulation are close.

'Asim read it by pausing on the lam of bal and beginning with the word ran, avoiding assimilation.

Hafs read it with a light pause (sakta) on the lam of bal, to show that it is a lam. Al-Lisan says: showing the lam (izhar) is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. Sibawayh said: both are good. Al-Zajjaj said: assimilation is more preferred.

Al-qulub are the minds and the places of perception. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has sealed upon their hearts﴾ [al-Baqara: 7] in Surat al-Baqara.

From the speech of the Bedouin herdsmen, who address their camels in the time of severe cold when they bring them to water and they recoil from it because of its coldness: "Barridiyhi tajidihi sakhinan" (cool it, you will find it hot), meaning: "bal raddiyhi" (rather, return it). This is one of the riddle-like witticisms (al-mulah al-shabiha bi al-mu'ayah), since its outward form seems to request cooling it, while in fact by cooling it, it will be found hot.

As for ﴿ma kanu yaksibun﴾, it means what they had done previously of evil deeds and their recklessness in refusing to reflect on the verses, until turning away and obstinacy became a deeply rooted disposition in them, so their minds do not comprehend the indication of the proofs for what they signify.

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "When the servant commits a sin, a black spot is made upon his heart. If he gives it up, seeks Allah's forgiveness, and repents, his heart is polished. But if he returns [to sin], it is increased until it covers his heart, and this is the ran that Allah mentioned in His Book: ﴿Kalla, bal ran 'ala qulubihim ma kanu yaksibun﴾." Al-Tirmidhi said: this is a hasan sahih hadith.

The use of the present form yaksibun instead of the past tense is to indicate the repetition and multiplicity of that earning in the past.

Mentioning the verb kanu instead of saying "ma yaksibun" is an indication that what is meant is what they earned during their lives of polytheism before the coming of Islam. For although they were not subject to legal responsibility (manat taklif) at that time, they opposed what the earlier revealed laws (al-shara'i' al-salifa) had brought, and what had been transmitted and spread among the nations of the call to the Oneness of Allah in divinity, according to the view of al-Ash'ari and Ahl al-Sunna regarding the basis for holding the people of the interval (ahl al-fatra) accountable for the sin of associating partners with Allah, as indicated by the proofs from the Book and the Sunna; or they opposed what clear reason requires, according to the view of al-Maturidi and the Mu'tazila. To this is added what they earned from the time of the coming of Islam until this surah was revealed, and that is a period that is not short.

The second kalla is an emphasis of the first kalla, increasing the rebuke so that it becomes a reproach.

Both meanings are intended here, because those who deny the Day of Judgement will not see God on the Day of Resurrection, when the people of faith will see Him.

This meaning is clarified by His words describing the condition of the righteous: ﴿Upon couches, gazing﴾ (al-Mutaffifin 83:35). Likewise, they will not enter the presence of holiness. This is an escalation in the threat, because it is a warning that they are among the people of the Fire, and that is more severe than the disgrace of humiliation.

*Sālū* is the plural of *sālin*, meaning one who has been touched by the heat of the Fire. It was discussed at the end of Surat al-Infitar.

The demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishara*, "this") implies that they have arrived at the punishment. Describing the punishment as that which they used to deny indicates that it is the punishment whose threat was repeated to them while they were denying it, and that is eternal abiding, which is a more severe degree of threat. For this reason the content of the conjoined sentence is what follows it.

﴿Indeed, the record of the righteous is in ʿIlliyyin﴾ ﴿And what can make you know what ʿIlliyyun is?﴾ ﴿It is a written record﴾ ﴿witnessed by those brought near [to Allah]﴾. So the correct view is that its meaning is a counterpart to the meaning of its like, so that the threat against the wicked is contrasted with the promise to the righteous. It is a habit of the Qur'an to follow a warning with glad tidings and vice versa, because people are both fearful and hopeful. Thus the mention of the bliss of the righteous is an insertion required by the context, even though the setting from the beginning of the surah is one of warning.

The speaker of the promise and the threat may be one and the same: He addressed His speech to the wicked who do not think they will be resurrected, and then followed it with a speech addressed to the righteous, who are the opposite of that. Having reproached them, they follow their reproach with a description of the bliss of the believers in the resurrection, as a censure of those who denied it and as a cause of regret for them over the good that they forfeited.

"Al-abrar" is the plural of barr (with a fatha on the ba'), who is one that performs birr (righteousness), and it was mentioned earlier in the previous surah.

The discussion of "al-kitab" (the record) and its being contained in ʿIlliyyin is like the discussion of ﴿Indeed, the record of the wicked is in Sijjin﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 7].

"ʿIlliyyun" is the plural of ʿIlliyy, and ʿIlliyy is on the pattern fiʿiyl from "al-ʿulluw" (elevation). It is an intensive form of description that came in the form of the sound masculine plural, and it is among the nouns that were attached to the sound masculine plural without analogical basis.

It is reported from al-Farra' that ʿIlliyyin has no singular. He means: ʿIlliyyin is not the plural of "ʿIlliyy," but rather a proper name for the place of the righteous in Paradise, since "ʿIlliyy" has not been heard from the Arabs; they only said "ʿIlliyyah" for an upper room, and ʿIlliyyun is a proper noun by predominance for the abode of the righteous.

It was formed in the pattern of the masculine plural because the original function of that pattern is to pluralize the names and attributes of rational beings, so the form of the plural of rational males was completed for it, to perfect the nobility of the meaning by the metaphor of elevation and the nobility of the category by giving it the form of the masculine.

It is reported from al-Farra' that ʿIlliyyin has no singular. He means: ʿIlliyyin is not the plural of "ʿIlliyy," but rather a proper name for the place of the righteous in Paradise, since "ʿIlliyy" has not been heard from the Arabs; they only said "ʿIlliyyah" for an upper room, and ʿIlliyyun is a proper noun by predominance for the abode of the righteous.

This name is derived from "al-ʿulluw" (elevation), and it is an elevation in rank, i.e., a height in the degrees of nobility and excellence. It was formed in the pattern of the masculine plural because the original function of that pattern is to pluralize the names and attributes of rational beings, so the form of the plural of rational males was completed for it, to perfect the nobility of the meaning by the metaphor of elevation and the nobility of the category by giving it the form of the masculine.

﴿And what can make you know what ʿIlliyyun is?﴾ The discussion of it is like the discussion of ﴿And what can make you know what Sijjin is? A written record﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 8] mentioned earlier.

﴿Witnessed﴾: they are informed of it, i.e., it is proclaimed in the presence of those brought near, who are the angels. This is a proclamation of honor for its owner, just as the names of the outstanding are proclaimed in teaching and the names of the heroes in the battalions.

Then the saying of that to them is a reproach and a rebuke for their neglect of faith.

Either of the two views does not conflict with the other regarding the particularities established for the sentence.

The righteous are mentioned by the explicit noun rather than by a pronoun, unlike what came in the sentence ﴿Indeed, they, from their Lord that Day, will be veiled﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 15], in order to draw attention to the quality of the righteous.

His saying ﴿on couches﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 35] is a second predicate (khabar thani) concerning the righteous, meaning: they are on couches, i.e., reclining upon them.

Al-arā'ik is the plural of arīka, on the pattern of safīna. The arīka is a name for a combination of a bed, its cushion, and a canopy erected over them both, so it is not said "arīka" except for the combination of these three. It has been said that it is Ethiopian (ḥabashiyya). This was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿reclining therein on couches﴾ [al-Insan: 13], in Surat al-Insan.

The object of yanẓurūna is omitted, either because of what preceded it, namely His saying concerning their opposites: ﴿Indeed, they, from their Lord that Day, will be veiled﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 15], and the implied meaning is: they gaze upon their Lord; or for the purpose of generality, meaning: they gaze upon everything that delights their souls and gladdens them, by the indication of the context of the seats of promise and honour.

Al-Jumhur (the majority) read taʿrifu (you recognize) in the active form with naṣb (accusative) on naḍrata (radiance). It is an address to an unspecified person, meaning: you recognize, O whoever sees them. Abu Jaʿfar and Yaʿqub read tuʿrafu (it is recognized) in the passive form with raf (nominative) on naḍratu.

The outcome of the two readings is one, except that the reading of the majority follows the particular manner of its usage, and the reading of Abu Jaʿfar and Yaʿqub follows the manner that is not specific to it.

Address in this manner, when describing great matters, is a well-known Arabic style. This sentence is a third predicate concerning the righteous, or a second circumstantial clause for them.

Al-naḍra is brightness and beauty, and the idafa (construction) of naḍra to al-naʿīm is an idafa of the effect to the cause, meaning: the radiance and brightness that appear on the face of one who is happy and content, when the signs of joy show upon his face.

He expressed it with yusqawna (they are given to drink) rather than yashrabūna (they drink), to indicate that they are served, with creatures serving them for that purpose in Paradise. That is part of the completeness of luxury and the pleasure of comfort.

Al-rahīq is a name for pure, good wine.

Al-makhtūm is the one whose vessel is sealed, i.e., its jar. It is the passive participle of khatama-hu, when one fastens it with a kind of clay known for its hardness when it dries, so that it is difficult to remove; and when it is removed, it becomes apparent that it has been unsealed. They used it to seal letters so that the carrier would not read what is in them. For this reason they say: "Part of the nobility of a letter is its sealing," and they make a mark upon it, which is impressed on it while it is still moist; when it dries, it becomes impossible to alter. What is impressed with is called khātam (signet) with a fatḥa on the taʾ. Kings, rulers and nobles used to make for themselves signet rings, which they placed on one of their little fingers, so that they would find them when issuing letters from them. Jarir said:

"It suffices the Caliph that God has clothed him
In the garment of kingship, by which the signets are guided."

They used to place the clay of sealing upon the place of closure of a bottle, a jar, or a wine jug, to prevent air from entering it, and this is better for its fermentation, for increasing its clarity, and for preserving its aroma. The sealing of the wine of Paradise was made with a paste of musk instead of sealing clay.

Musk is an animal substance with a famous fragrance, whose good scent and strong smell have been well known since ancient times. This substance forms in a gland filled with blood that protrudes from the neck of a species of gazelle in the lands of Tibet, from the land of China. It remains attached to its neck until it dries and falls off; then its seekers pick it up and trade in it. It is a membrane in the shape of a small mouse, and for this reason they say: "the musk mouse."

"Of what is aged in the tavern by the one who plucks it,
Sealed with the brown pepper and pomegranate."

That is: it ends with the sharpness of pepper and the taste of pomegranate.

The sentence ﴿and for that let the competitors compete﴾ is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyya) between the sentence ﴿whose seal is musk﴾ and the sentence ﴿and its mixture is from Tasnim﴾.

Know that the structure of this sentence is subtle and needs explanation: we take the waw (and) as parenthetical. His saying "wa-fī dhālika" (and for that) is the beginning of the sentence. The fronting of the prepositional phrase serves to express restriction (ḥaṣr), meaning: and for that nectar let people compete, not for the nectar of this world for which the people of luxury compete, bringing it from the far reaches of the lands and spending wealth on it. Since the waw was parenthetical, there was no difficulty in the response particle fa- (then) occurring after it. The fa- may be either eloquent (faṣīḥa), with the implied meaning: if you know the descriptions of this nectar, then let the competitors compete for it; or the implied meaning is: and for that, compete, so let the competitors compete for it. Then the sentence has the force of a concluding statement (tadhyīl), because what is implied is the competing of the addressees, and what is stated is the competing of all competitors, so it is generalization after specification. Or the fa- may be the response particle to an implied condition in the speech, which is indicated by the fronting of the prepositional phrase, because the fronting of the prepositional phrase is often treated like a conditional, as was narrated in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "As you are, so you will be ruled over," with the verbs "takūnū" and "yuwalla" in the jussive. The implied meaning is: if you know that, then let the competitors compete for it. Or the fa- may be a branching off from an omitted element according to the method of omission under the condition of interpretation, the implied meaning being: "And compete for that," in the form of an imperative; and the speech then indicates the emphasis of the verb of competition, since it is in the position of being mentioned twice, along with the expression of specificity through the fronting of the prepositional phrase.

The sentence ﴿and for that let the competitors compete﴾ is parenthetical between the sentence ﴿they will be given to drink from nectar﴾ etc. and the sentence ﴿and its mixture is from Tasnim﴾.

Al-tanāfus (competition) is a reciprocal form from nafisa ʿalayhi bi-kadhā, when one is stingy with something toward another and does not regard him as worthy of it. It is from the derivation of a thing that is precious (nafīs), which is the elevated one in its kind, desired to attain. It has been said that the original root of this material is the soul (nafs). So tanāfus is the attainment of preciousness among several parties.

The imperative lām in "fa-l-yatanāfasi" (then let them compete) is used to urge and incite.

Mizājuhu (its mixture) is that with which it is mixed. Its origin is the verbal noun of māzaja, meaning mazaja, and it was applied to what is mixed with it, so it is the application of the verbal noun to the object. They used to mix wine so that its violence would not overpower them and the disappearance of their reason would not come upon them swiftly, because they intended to prolong the portion of intoxication for enjoyment of the creeping of drunkenness into the mind, without it overwhelming them suddenly. For this reason, the aged pure wine is most often drunk mixed with water. Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

"It was mixed with what has a sharp taste, from water in a skin,
Clear, in al-Abtah, which is now mixed."

And Ḥassān said:

"They give to drink to whoever comes to al-Buraydh among them,
From the Barada that is stirred with the smooth nectar."

Their competition for wine is well known among their customs, and their poetry overflows with it, like the saying of Labid:

"I boil the cooking pot with every dark, aged jar,
Or with a jug that was opened and whose seal was removed."

Tasnīm is a proper name for a spring in Paradise, derived from the verbal noun of sanama al-shay, when he made it like the shape of a hump (sanām). They explained this naming by saying that this spring pours down upon their gardens from above, so it is like a hump. This name is Arabic in its root and pattern, but it was not known among the Arabs, so it is among the things the Qur'an informed about. For this reason Ibn ʿAbbas, when asked about it, said: "This is among what God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿No soul knows what has been hidden for them of comfort for their eyes﴾ [al-Sajda: 17]," meaning they do not know the things or their names except what God has informed them of. Because of its strangeness, it needed clarification by His saying: ﴿a spring from which those brought near will drink﴾, meaning: Tasnīm being a spring from which those brought near will drink.

Al-muqarrabūn (those brought near) are the righteous, meaning: those who drink from this water are the brought near.

The bāʾ in ﴿from which will drink﴾ is either causal (sababiyya), and the verb yashrabu has been made to take the pronoun of the spring as its object by implying the meaning of yamzuju (to mix), in His saying: ﴿and its mixture is from Tasnim﴾, meaning: they mix the nectar with Tasnim. Or it is the bāʾ of accompaniment (mulābasa), and the verb yashrabu is transitive to an omitted object, which is the nectar, meaning: they drink the nectar while in contact with the spring, i.e., surrounding it and sitting around it. "They drank with the water of the sea, then rose up,
Where there are seas, green, and for them there is a roaring."

The intense eagerness to say, "Indeed these people are astray," whenever they see them, resembles the state of one who has been sent to follow up on someone's affairs. It is part of the messenger's nature to be eager to convey the message.

The statement is used in the sense of mockery (*tahakkum*, ridicule) toward the polytheists. That is, they were not appointed to watch over them and to take care of their rectitude.

Thus the meaning of "guarding" (*hifz*) here is supervision (*raqabah*). For this reason it is followed by the preposition ʿalā, so that the negation applies to both the sending and the guarding, and the figurative sense of elevation (*isti'la'*) conveyed by the particle ʿalā negates their depicted state.

Placing the prepositional phrase before the word it governs is for emphasis on the meaning of the particle of elevation and its object, while observing the rhyme of the verse-ending (*fasilah*).

The particle *fa* of causation in His saying, ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾, indicates that their mockery of the believers in this world was a cause of their being repaid in the Hereafter with something of the same kind, since God made those who believed laugh at the polytheists. So it was a fitting recompense (*jaza' wifaqan*).

Placing "today" (*al-yawm*) before "laugh" is for emphasis on it, because it is the day of the great, eternal recompense. His saying, ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾, is obscure in its connection to what precedes it in the arrangement of the discourse, and all the exegetes remained silent about it except Ibn ʿAtiyyah. The reason is that defining "today" with the article *al-*, while it is an accusative adverbial of time, requires that "today" refers to a present day at the time the verse was revealed, like the time of the speaker's utterance. If one says, "Today such-and-such will happen," it is necessarily understood that he is speaking of his present day. Therefore the laughter of those who believed at the disbelievers does not occur at the time the verse was revealed, but happens on the Day of Recompense. It is not sound to interpret His saying "so today" as meaning "so on the Day of Resurrection those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers," for if that were the case, the expected wording would be: "So on that day those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers."

Ibn ʿAtiyyah sensed this difficulty and said:

"Since the preceding verses were linked to the Day of Resurrection, and since woe on that day is for those who deny, it was permissible to say 'so today' as a relating of what is said on that day and what will occur." End of quote.

This is a spark that needs kindling wood to catch fire.

Rather, we may connect what precedes it to the speech that will be addressed to them on the Day of Resurrection beginning from His saying, ﴿Then it will be said, "This is what you used to deny"﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 17], up to here, as already explained.

The implied meaning is: "And it will be said to them today: those who believed will laugh at you."

The subject is placed before the predicate verb in His saying, ﴿Those who believed among the disbelievers laugh﴾, rather than saying, "So today those who believed laugh," in order to indicate restriction (*hasr*, exclusivity). It is a restriction of specification (*qasr idafi*) in contrast to His saying, ﴿They used to laugh at those who believed﴾. That is: the mockery of the polytheists toward the believers has ceased, so today the believers laugh at the disbelievers, and not the reverse.

Placing "among the disbelievers" before its governed element, "laugh," is for emphasis on the one being laughed at, to hasten their distress upon hearing this rebuke.

His saying, ﴿among the disbelievers﴾, is an explicit noun in the place of a pronoun. It was avoided to say "they laugh at them," because the explicit descriptive phrase carries a rebuke of the disbelievers.

The object of "they look" (*yanzurun*) is elided, indicated by His saying, ﴿among the disbelievers laugh﴾. The implied meaning is: "they look," that is, they behold the polytheists in punishment and humiliation.

The polytheists, out of their arrogance, used to mock the believers, most of whom were the weak people of Mecca, and so they laughed at them. Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 83, verses 29–35 (part 2 of 2):

The clause ﴿and they were not sent as guardians over them﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: they slander them with misguidance while they were not sent by anyone as guardians over their deeds. This indicates that their state is like the state of one who has been sent. For this reason it is negated that they were sent as guardians over them. The intense eagerness to say, "Indeed these people are astray," whenever they see them, resembles the state of one who has been sent to follow up on someone's affairs. It is part of the messenger's nature to be eager to convey the message.

The statement is used in the sense of mockery (*tahakkum*, ridicule) toward the polytheists. That is, they were not appointed to watch over them and to take care of their rectitude.

Thus the meaning of "guarding" (*hifz*) here is supervision (*raqabah*). For this reason it is followed by the preposition ʿalā, so that the negation applies to both the sending and the guarding, and the figurative sense of elevation (*isti'la'*) conveyed by the particle ʿalā negates their depicted state.

Placing the prepositional phrase before the word it governs is for emphasis on the meaning of the particle of elevation and its object, while observing the rhyme of the verse-ending (*fasilah*).

The particle *fa* of causation in His saying, ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾, indicates that their mockery of the believers in this world was a cause of their being repaid in the Hereafter with something of the same kind, since God made those who believed laugh at the polytheists. So it was a fitting recompense (*jaza' wifaqan*).

Placing "today" (*al-yawm*) before "laugh" is for emphasis on it, because it is the day of the great, eternal recompense. His saying, ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾, is obscure in its connection to what precedes it in the arrangement of the discourse, and all the exegetes remained silent about it except Ibn ʿAtiyyah. The reason is that defining "today" with the article *al-*, while it is an accusative adverbial of time, requires that "today" refers to a present day at the time the verse was revealed, like the time of the speaker's utterance. If one says, "Today such-and-such will happen," it is necessarily understood that he is speaking of his present day. Therefore the laughter of those who believed at the disbelievers does not occur at the time the verse was revealed, but happens on the Day of Recompense. It is not sound to interpret His saying "so today" as meaning "so on the Day of Resurrection those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers," for if that were the case, the expected wording would be: "So on that day those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers."

Ibn ʿAtiyyah sensed this difficulty and said:

"Since the preceding verses were linked to the Day of Resurrection, and since woe on that day is for those who deny, it was permissible to say 'so today' as a relating of what is said on that day and what will occur." End of quote.

This is a spark that needs kindling wood to catch fire.

Rather, we may connect what precedes it to the speech that will be addressed to them on the Day of Resurrection beginning from His saying, ﴿Then it will be said, "This is what you used to deny"﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 17], up to here, as already explained.

Or we may take His saying, ﴿So today those who believed﴾ etc., as the object of an elided speech, indicated by His saying in the preceding verse, ﴿Then it will be said, "This is what you used to deny"﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 17]. The implied meaning is: "And it will be said to them today: those who believed will laugh at you."

The subject is placed before the predicate verb in His saying, ﴿Those who believed among the disbelievers laugh﴾, rather than saying, "So today those who believed laugh," in order to indicate restriction (*hasr*, exclusivity). It is a restriction of specification (*qasr idafi*) in contrast to His saying, ﴿They used to laugh at those who believed﴾. That is: the mockery of the polytheists toward the believers has ceased, so today the believers laugh at the disbelievers, and not the reverse.

Placing "among the disbelievers" before its governed element, "laugh," is for emphasis on the one being laughed at, to hasten their distress upon hearing this rebuke.

His saying, ﴿among the disbelievers﴾, is an explicit noun in the place of a pronoun. It was avoided to say "they laugh at them," because the explicit descriptive phrase carries a rebuke of the disbelievers.

The object of "they look" (*yanzurun*) is elided, indicated by His saying, ﴿among the disbelievers laugh﴾. The implied meaning is: "they look," that is, they behold the polytheists in punishment and humiliation.

"Idhā" in the three places is used for past time, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor [is there blame] upon those who, when they came to you that you might give them mounts, you said, "I find not that upon which I can mount you," and they turned back while their eyes overflowed with tears from grief﴾ [al-Tawba: 92], and His saying: ﴿And when there comes to them a matter about security or fear, they spread it around﴾ [al-Nisa: 83].

The purpose of mentioning it is that, after He had mentioned the state of the polytheists separately and the state of the Muslims separately, He followed with what contains a description of the outcome of the polytheists in their treatment of the believers in this world, so that both groups would know their recompense together.

The issuing of that speech on the Day of Resurrection is used for reproach and rebuke, as its gist requires from His saying: ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾ to the end of the surah.

The opening with ﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes﴾ in the form of an emphasized statement serves to convey the importance of the speech; this is common at the beginning of a speech whose announcement is intended, so that all listeners are directed by that opening to listen to it, indicating that it is an important report. What is meant by ﴿those who committed crimes﴾ is the polytheists of Mecca, and especially their chieftains.

They are: Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, ʿUqba ibn Abi Muʿayt, al-ʿAs ibn Wa'il, al-Aswad ibn ʿAbd Yaghuth, al-ʿAs ibn Hisham, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith. They used to laugh at ʿAmmar ibn Yasir, Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, Bilal, and Suhayb, and they used to mock them.

He expressed it with the relative pronoun and this relative clause, ﴿those who committed crimes﴾, to draw attention to the fact that what He reports about them is a crime, and so that the placement of His saying ﴿Have the disbelievers been rewarded for what they used to do?﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 36] may become clear.

Ijram (crime) means committing a jurm, which is a great sin; and the greatest of crimes is disbelief. The construction "kanu yadhakūn" indicates that this is a constant trait of theirs in the past, and the use of the present form "yadhakūn" indicates the recurrence of this from them and that it is their habit.

The transitive construction of the verb "yadhakūn" to the cause of laughter with the preposition "min", which is the most common in the transitivity of verbs of this root, is based on "min" being initial (ibtida'iyya), which makes the state that prompts laughter resemble a place from which laughter originates. Similar are the verbs "sakhira minhu" and "ʿajiba minhu".

The meaning of "yadhakūna minhum" is: they laugh at their condition. The polytheists, out of their arrogance, used to mock the believers, most of whom were the weak people of Mecca, and so they laughed at them. Apparently this took place in their gatherings when they spoke of their condition, in contrast to His saying: ﴿And when they passed by them, they winked at one another﴾.

Know that when the cause of laughter is a particular state among states, the object of the preposition is the noun of that state, as in ﴿So he smiled, laughing at her speech﴾ [al-Naml: 19], and when it is the totality of a thing's form, the object of the preposition is the noun of the entity possessing the states, because the noun of the entity is more comprehensive of what is known of its states, as in ﴿And you used to laugh at them﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 110], and the verse of ʿAbd Yaghuth al-Harithi:

"And a shaykha of the ʿAbshams laughs at me, as if she had never seen before me a Yemeni captive."

Al-taghamuz is a reciprocal form from al-ghamz, and it is applied to touching a thing with the hand with firm pressure, and from it is pressing the spear to straighten it and removing its knots. In the hadith of ʿA'isha: "I saw myself while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was praying and I was lying between him and the qibla, and when he wanted to prostrate he pressed my leg, and I drew them in."

Al-ghamz is also applied to moving the eye with the intention of alerting the viewer to what he might miss seeing of the circumstances of the situation. Both usages are valid for interpreting the meaning of the verse.

The pronoun in "marru" may refer back to "those who committed crimes", in which case the pronoun in "bihim" refers to "those who believed", and the reverse is also permissible. As for the pronoun in "yataghamazun", it is exclusively referring to "those who committed crimes".

The meaning: when the believers passed by those who committed crimes while they were in their gatherings, the criminals would wink at one another at the moment of the believers' passing; or, when those who committed crimes passed by those who believed while they were at their work and in the hardship of their circumstances, the criminals would wink at one another at the moment of their passing. They wink without openly announcing the mockery of them, to avoid the believers' retaliation with abuse, since the believers were then numerous in Mecca at the time this surah was revealed,

Al-inqilab: returning to the place from which one came. It is said: "The traveler returned (inqalaba) to his family," and in the travel supplication: "I seek refuge in You from the grief of returning (al-munqalab)." Its origin is a metaphor from turning a garment, when one turns it from its face to another face. It is said: "He turned (qalaba) the thing" when he returned it.

The "ahl" of a man is his wife and his children, and "ahl" is mentioned here because they are the ones with whom one relaxes in conversation; therefore it is said "to their families" rather than "to their houses."

The meaning: when those who committed crimes returned to their homes and were alone with their families, they conversed with them in pleasantries, mentioning the believers and disparaging them.

The repetition of the verb "inqalabu" in His saying "inqalabu fakihin" is among the sturdy constructions of speech. It would have been sufficient to say, "And when they returned to their families, they were jesting," or "and when they returned to their families they were jesting." This is because repeating the verb adds further confirmation of its meaning in the hearer's mind, since it is something that deserves attention, and to add to the confirmation of what the verb conveys of renewal, so that there is an evocation of the state. Ibn Jinni said in his book al-Tanbih ʿala Iʿrab al-Hamasa, regarding the verse of al-Ahwas:

"So when he moves, he moves away from a raging one whose outbursts are feared by his rivals."

It is impossible to say "idha qumtu qumtu" and "idha aqʿudu aqʿudu," because there is nothing in the second but what is in the first; that is, it is not correct to make the second an answer to the first. What permitted saying "fa-idha tazulu tazulu" is the preposition attached to the second verb, which conveys the benefit. A similar example is God's saying: ﴿These are those whom We led astray; We led them astray as We were astray﴾ [al-Qasas: 63]. If He had said, "These are those whom We led astray; We led them astray," the statement would have conveyed nothing, since it is like your saying, "The one I struck, I struck," or "The one I honored, I honored." Abu ʿAli had refrained in this verse from what we have taken, but the matter in it, in my view, is as I have explained to you. End of quote.

This was discussed in Surat al-Qasas and in Surat al-Furqan.

The sentence "And when they saw them, they said, 'Indeed, these are misguided'" reports what those who committed crimes say about the believers when they see them; that is, they combine harm through gestures and demeanor and evil speech in their absence, and evil speech publicly in the hearing of the believers, in the hope that they will return from Islam to disbelief. Their intended meaning by "misguidance" is corruption of judgment, because the polytheists do not recognize legal misguidance. That is, "these are people of corrupt judgment, for they followed Islam and broke away from their people, and neglected the pleasures of this life in hope of a pleasure after death, and devoted themselves to prayer and to the morals that the polytheists regard as illusions and folly, since they are far from grasping the measure of perfect spiritual excellence, and their only concern was bodily pleasure."

The word "idha" in one of the three sentences is an adverb connected to the verb that follows it in each sentence.

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 83, verses 29–35 (part 2 of 2):

The clause ﴿and they were not sent as guardians over them﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: they slander them with misguidance while they were not sent by anyone as guardians over their deeds. This indicates that their state is like the state of one who has been sent. For this reason it is negated that they were sent as guardians over them. The intense eagerness to say, "Indeed these people are astray," whenever they see them, resembles the state of one who has been sent to follow up on someone's affairs. It is part of the messenger's nature to be eager to convey the message.

The statement is used in the sense of mockery (*tahakkum*, ridicule) toward the polytheists. That is, they were not appointed to watch over them and to take care of their rectitude.

Thus the meaning of "guarding" (*hifz*) here is supervision (*raqabah*). For this reason it is followed by the preposition ʿalā, so that the negation applies to both the sending and the guarding, and the figurative sense of elevation (*isti'la'*) conveyed by the particle ʿalā negates their depicted state.

Placing the prepositional phrase before the word it governs is for emphasis on the meaning of the particle of elevation and its object, while observing the rhyme of the verse-ending (*fasilah*).

The particle *fa* of causation in His saying, ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾, indicates that their mockery of the believers in this world was a cause of their being repaid in the Hereafter with something of the same kind, since God made those who believed laugh at the polytheists. So it was a fitting recompense (*jaza' wifaqan*).

Placing "today" (*al-yawm*) before "laugh" is for emphasis on it, because it is the day of the great, eternal recompense. His saying, ﴿So today those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers﴾, is obscure in its connection to what precedes it in the arrangement of the discourse, and all the exegetes remained silent about it except Ibn ʿAtiyyah. The reason is that defining "today" with the article *al-*, while it is an accusative adverbial of time, requires that "today" refers to a present day at the time the verse was revealed, like the time of the speaker's utterance. If one says, "Today such-and-such will happen," it is necessarily understood that he is speaking of his present day. Therefore the laughter of those who believed at the disbelievers does not occur at the time the verse was revealed, but happens on the Day of Recompense. It is not sound to interpret His saying "so today" as meaning "so on the Day of Resurrection those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers," for if that were the case, the expected wording would be: "So on that day those who believed will laugh at the disbelievers."

Ibn ʿAtiyyah sensed this difficulty and said:

"Since the preceding verses were linked to the Day of Resurrection, and since woe on that day is for those who deny, it was permissible to say 'so today' as a relating of what is said on that day and what will occur." End of quote.

This is a spark that needs kindling wood to catch fire.

Rather, we may connect what precedes it to the speech that will be addressed to them on the Day of Resurrection beginning from His saying, ﴿Then it will be said, "This is what you used to deny"﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 17], up to here, as already explained.

Or we may take His saying, ﴿So today those who believed﴾ etc., as the object of an elided speech, indicated by His saying in the preceding verse, ﴿Then it will be said, "This is what you used to deny"﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 17]. The implied meaning is: "And it will be said to them today: those who believed will laugh at you."

The subject is placed before the predicate verb in His saying, ﴿Those who believed among the disbelievers laugh﴾, rather than saying, "So today those who believed laugh," in order to indicate restriction (*hasr*, exclusivity). It is a restriction of specification (*qasr idafi*) in contrast to His saying, ﴿They used to laugh at those who believed﴾. That is: the mockery of the polytheists toward the believers has ceased, so today the believers laugh at the disbelievers, and not the reverse.

Placing "among the disbelievers" before its governed element, "laugh," is for emphasis on the one being laughed at, to hasten their distress upon hearing this rebuke.

His saying, ﴿among the disbelievers﴾, is an explicit noun in the place of a pronoun. It was avoided to say "they laugh at them," because the explicit descriptive phrase carries a rebuke of the disbelievers.

The object of "they look" (*yanzurun*) is elided, indicated by His saying, ﴿among the disbelievers laugh﴾. The implied meaning is: "they look," that is, they behold the polytheists in punishment and humiliation.

**Commentary on 83:36**

﴿Has the disbelievers been recompensed for what they used to do?﴾

This is a concluding summary (fadhlaka) of what was recounted about the aggression of the polytheists against the believers and the requital that follows it on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is: the disbelievers have indeed been recompensed for what they used to do. This is part of the completion of the announcement (nida') that will be attached to them on the Day of Resurrection.

The interrogation with *hal* is affirmative (taqriri), and it expresses astonishment at the fact that they could not escape it after long ages.

[p. 216 continues]

The interrogation is of the type of *talab* (request), so it is one of the forms of address (khitab). The address in this question is directed to no specific person, but to everyone who hears that announcement on the Day of Resurrection. This is part of what is said by an omitted speaker (maqul al-qawl al-mahdhuf).

*Thuwwiba* means "was given reward." It is said *thawwabahu*, just as it is said *athabahu*, when one gives him a reward (thawab).

*Thawab* is what one is recompensed with, of good, for a praiseworthy deed. This is its real meaning, as in *al-Sihah*, and it is the apparent meaning in *al-Asas*. Therefore its use here for the recompense of evil is a sarcastic metaphor (isti'arah tahakkumiyyah). This is the verified view, and it is what al-Raghib explicitly stated at the end of his discussion when he said that it is used for the recompense of both good and evil. He meant that it is used metaphorically for the recompense of evil frequently, so there must be a relation (`alaqah) and an indicator (qarinah). Here the indicator is His saying "the disbelievers" and "what they used to do," as in the saying of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

*You alighted at our dwelling as guests among us, so we hastened the hospitality before you could revile us.*

*We hosted you, and hastened your entertainment before the dawn, with a grinding millstone.*

And of the same kind is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 24].

*Ma kanu yaf'aluna* is a relative clause (mawsul), and it is the second object of the verb *thuwwiba*, since it is of the pattern of *a'ta*. The recompense is not itself what they used to do; rather it is expressed by this relative clause because of its equating the severity of their crime, by way of eloquent comparison (tashbih baligh), or by omission of a modifier whose estimated word is "like" (mithl). It is also permissible that it be by removal of the preposition, which is the causal *ba'* (bi), meaning: "for what they used to do."

In this sentence there is the embellishment of *bara'at al-maqta'* (the excellence of the conclusion), because it comprises what the surah contains.

**Surah al-Inshiqaq**

It was named in the time of the Companions "Surah Idha as-sama'u inshaqqat." The commentators and the writers of the codices (masahif) named it "Surat al-Inshiqaq" according to its meaning, just as the preceding surah was named "Surat al-Tatfif" and "Surat Inshaqqat" in abbreviation.

Al-Ja'bari mentioned it in his *Nazm* in the enumeration of the Meccan and Medinan surahs with the word *kadh*, so it is possible that he meant that this is its name. I have not found this for anyone else.

It is not mentioned in *al-Itqan* among the surahs with more than one name.

It is Meccan by consensus.

It is counted as the eighty-third in the enumeration of the order of the revelation of surahs. It was revealed after Surat al-Infitar and before Surat al-Rum.

The scholars of counting (ahl al-'adad) counted its verses as twenty-five in Medina, Mecca and Kufa, and the people of Basra and Syria counted them as twenty-three.
